## 10.4 Choosing a decision threshold

The default threshold of 0.5 is not always clinically appropriate. Missing a patient who will die (a false negative) may cost more than a false alarm, so the threshold can be chosen separately from the model.

The threshold is chosen on the **out-of-fold cross-validated predictions** (`fit_final$pred`, kept by `savePredictions = "final"`). Each training patient was predicted by a model that never saw that patient, so these probabilities are honest. Predictions
of the final model on its own training patients would be over-confident and would give a biased threshold. Here the threshold maximises Youden's index (sensitivity + specificity − 1), which weights both error types equally; a clinical application could
instead require a minimum sensitivity. The chosen threshold is then evaluated **once** on the test set.

```{r final-threshold}
# Out-of-fold predictions of the chosen tuning setting: one row per training patient
oof <- fit_final$pred
stopifnot(nrow(oof) == nrow(tr_DF))

roc_cv <- pROC::roc(oof$obs, oof$Died, levels = c("Survived", "Died"), direction = "<", quiet = TRUE)

thr <- pROC::coords(roc_cv, x = "best", best.method = "youden",
                    ret = "threshold", transpose = FALSE)
thr <- as.numeric(thr$threshold)[1]

# Cross-validated sensitivity / specificity / accuracy at the chosen threshold
cv_at_thr <- pROC::coords(roc_cv, x = thr, input = "threshold",
                          ret = c("sensitivity", "specificity"), transpose = FALSE)
cv_acc <- mean((oof$Died >= thr) == (oof$obs == "Died"))

# Test set: default threshold versus the cross-validated threshold
te_class_thr <- factor(ifelse(te_prob >= thr, "Died", "Survived"), levels = c("Died", "Survived"))
cm_te_thr <- caret::confusionMatrix(te_class_thr, te_DF[[y_col]], positive = "Died")

tibble(Evaluation = c("Cross-validation (threshold chosen here)", "Test, default threshold", "Test, chosen threshold"),
       Threshold   = c(thr, 0.5, thr),
       Sensitivity = c(cv_at_thr$sensitivity, cm_te$byClass[["Sensitivity"]], cm_te_thr$byClass[["Sensitivity"]]),
       Specificity = c(cv_at_thr$specificity, cm_te$byClass[["Specificity"]], cm_te_thr$byClass[["Specificity"]]),
       Accuracy    = c(cv_acc, cm_te$overall[["Accuracy"]], cm_te_thr$overall[["Accuracy"]])) %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Effect of the decision threshold (chosen on cross-validated predictions)")
```

# 11. Discussion

## 11.1 What the dataset implies for modelling

The choice of algorithm should follow the structure of the data. The features of this cohort that matter most are:

**Moderate sample size:** `r nrow(tr_DF)` training patients (`r sum(tr_DF[[y_col]] == "Died")` deaths and `r sum(tr_DF[[y_col]] == "Survived")` survivors) for `r length(X_cols)` predictors. This is enough for simple and regularised models, but not for very
flexible ones, which tend to fit noise.

**Many weak or uninformative predictors:** Roughly half of the genes, SNPs and imaging features carry little independent information about death. Methods that shrink or ignore such predictors have an advantage.

**Correlated blocks:** Gene expression, the derived scores and the radiomics features move together (several pairs with \|r\| above 0.7, see the correlation plot). Models differ strongly in how they treat redundant information.

**Mostly additive effects:** The main clinical and biological effects act roughly additively on the log-odds of death, with only minor non-linear terms and interactions (the outcome was simulated in `scripts/simulate_hnscc_data.py`). Linear models match
this structure; flexible models have to learn it.

**Mixed predictor types:** Continuous, skewed, binary, count (SNP) and ordinal predictors, handled by the recipe (dummy coding, Yeo-Johnson, scaling).

**Mild class imbalance:** About `r f2(100 * mean(tr_DF[[y_col]] == "Died"))`% of patients died, so a vote-based or threshold-based rule at 0.5 leans towards the majority class (survival).

## 11.2 How the models differ

| Model | Core idea | Decision boundary | Treatment of correlated predictors | Main safeguard against over-fitting | Main risk on this dataset |
|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| `glmnet` | Logistic regression with an elastic-net penalty | Linear in the log-odds | Ridge part shares weight; lasso part selects | `alpha`, `lambda` | Cannot find interactions or non-linear effects |
| `pls` | Regress on a few latent components that maximise covariance with the outcome | Linear | Built for collinearity | Number of components | Scores are not true probabilities; ignores non-linearity |
| `rda` | Gaussian classes; `lambda` blends class-specific and pooled covariances (LDA at 1), `gamma` shrinks towards a diagonal | Linear to quadratic | Models the full covariance | `gamma`, `lambda` | Gaussian assumption; noisy covariances |
| `nb` | Product of marginal class-conditional densities | Non-linear marginals, no interactions | Assumes independence, so double counts | Smoothing, bandwidth | Over-confident probabilities |
| `knn` | Majority vote of the k most similar patients | Local, non-parametric | Redundant predictors inflate distances | `k` | Curse of dimensionality |
| `pam` | Class centroids shrunk by soft-thresholding | Linear (diagonal covariance) | Ignores correlation | Shrinkage threshold | Designed for p much larger than n |
| `gbm` | Sequence of shallow trees fitted to the logistic-loss gradient | Non-linear, interactions | Robust | Depth, shrinkage, trees | Needs many steps to approximate smooth effects |
| `xgbTree` | Regularised boosted trees with sampling | Non-linear, interactions | Robust; column subsampling | `gamma`, `eta`, subsampling, depth | As `gbm`, but more regularised |
| `nnet` | One hidden layer with weight decay | Non-linear | Shared hidden units | Weight decay, few units | Local optima, start-dependent |
| `mlp` | One hidden layer trained by back-propagation | Non-linear | Shared hidden units | Number of units only | Higher variance, random starts |

## 11.3 Model by Model

```{r disc-prep}
# Helpers and summary quantities used in the text below
cv_auc <- function(m) if (m %in% cv_tbl$Model)  f3(cv_tbl$ROC[cv_tbl$Model == m])  else "n/a"
te_auc <- function(m) if (m %in% perf_te$Model) f3(perf_te$AUC[perf_te$Model == m]) else "n/a"
tr_auc <- function(m) if (m %in% perf_tr$Model) f3(perf_tr$AUC[perf_tr$Model == m]) else "n/a"

gap_tbl <- cv_tbl %>%
  select(Model, `CV AUC` = ROC, Sensitivity, Specificity) %>%
  left_join(perf_tr %>% select(Model, `Train AUC` = AUC), by = "Model") %>%
  left_join(perf_te %>% select(Model, `Test AUC` = AUC), by = "Model") %>%
  mutate(`Train - CV gap` = `Train AUC` - `CV AUC`,
         `CV - Test gap`  = `CV AUC` - `Test AUC`) %>%
  arrange(desc(`CV AUC`))

best_cv        <- max(cv_tbl$ROC)
near_best      <- cv_tbl$Model[cv_tbl$ROC >= best_cv - 0.01]
worst_model    <- cv_tbl$Model[which.min(cv_tbl$ROC)]
auc_range      <- diff(range(cv_tbl$ROC))
hi_spec_model  <- cv_tbl$Model[which.max(cv_tbl$Specificity)]
lo_sens_model  <- cv_tbl$Model[which.min(cv_tbl$Sensitivity)]
hi_sens_model  <- cv_tbl$Model[which.max(cv_tbl$Sensitivity)]
big_gap_model  <- gap_tbl$Model[which.max(gap_tbl$`Train - CV gap`)]
big_gap        <- max(gap_tbl$`Train - CV gap`)
small_gap_model <- gap_tbl$Model[which.min(gap_tbl$`Train - CV gap`)]
small_gap      <- min(gap_tbl$`Train - CV gap`)
rank_cor       <- cor(gap_tbl$`CV AUC`, gap_tbl$`Test AUC`, method = "spearman")

roc_cols <- grep("~ROC$", names(rs$values), value = TRUE)
fold_sd  <- median(sapply(rs$values[roc_cols], sd))      # typical fold-to-fold SD of the AUC
```

### Penalised and latent-variable linear models

**Elastic-net logistic regression (`glmnet`):** The model is an ordinary logistic regression whose coefficients are shrunk by a mixture of an L1 (lasso) and an L2 (ridge) penalty. The lasso part sets weak coefficients exactly to zero; the ridge part
spreads weight across correlated predictors instead of giving all of it to one. This is well matched to the cohort: many predictors are weak, several are redundant, and the strongest effects are additive on the log-odds scale. Shrinkage lowers variance,
and the logistic likelihood gives well-calibrated probabilities. Its weakness is that it can only see interactions and non-linear effects if they are supplied. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("glmnet")`, test AUC `r te_auc("glmnet")`.

**Partial least squares (`pls`):** Instead of using each predictor separately, PLS builds a small number of latent components, weighted combinations of the predictors that covary most with the outcome, and regresses on them. The gene, score and radiomics
blocks collapse onto a few components, which stabilises the fit; a small number of components is usually enough here. Because it is a regularised linear model, its discrimination is close to `glmnet`. It differs in that the component scores are converted
into class probabilities by a softmax rule, which are usually less well calibrated than logistic probabilities, and the components are not optimised for the likelihood. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("pls")`, test AUC `r te_auc("pls")`.

### Discriminant and probabilistic models

**Regularised discriminant analysis (`rda`):** Each class (died, survived) is described as a multivariate normal distribution. A new patient is assigned to the class under which the predictors are more likely. The parameter `lambda` blends class-specific
covariance matrices (`lambda = 0`, a quadratic boundary) with a single pooled matrix (`lambda = 1`, a linear boundary, as in linear discriminant analysis), and `gamma` shrinks the covariance further towards a diagonal matrix. With
`r sum(tr_DF[[y_col]] == "Died")` deaths and `r length(X_cols)` predictors, class-specific covariance matrices are noisy, so a pooled covariance is expected to win. A linear discriminant is nearly equivalent to logistic regression when the class
covariances are similar, which explains why `rda` performs close to `glmnet`. The Gaussian assumption is violated by the 0/1 and count predictors, but they carry limited signal, so the cost is small. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("rda")`, test AUC
`r te_auc("rda")`.

**Naive Bayes (`nb`)**: Naive Bayes multiplies the class-conditional density of every predictor, estimated here with a kernel smoother, as if the predictors were independent given the outcome. That assumption fails in this cohort: the gene-expression
block, the derived scores and the radiomics features are strongly correlated, so the same evidence is counted several times. The result is over-confident probabilities and a weaker ranking of patients. The many uninformative predictors each add a little
noise to the product. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("nb")`, test AUC `r te_auc("nb")`.

### Distance- and centroid-based models

**k-nearest neighbours (`knn`):** A patient is classified by a vote among the k most similar training patients in the standardised predictor space. There is no model to fit, and no way to down-weight irrelevant predictors: with `r length(X_cols)`
dimensions, about half of them uninformative, distances are dominated by noise, and close neighbours are few (the curse of dimensionality). Probabilities are multiples of 1/k, which makes the ranking coarse and limits the AUC. Because most neighbours of an
uncertain patient are survivors, the vote leans towards the majority class, which raises specificity and lowers sensitivity at the 0.5 threshold. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("knn")`, test AUC `r te_auc("knn")`.

**Nearest shrunken centroids (`pam`)**: The method computes a centroid for each class and shrinks each predictor's centroid difference towards zero by a threshold, removing predictors whose difference falls to zero. It then assigns a patient to the nearest
centroid. It was designed for gene-expression data with thousands of predictors and few samples, where selection is essential. Here there are far more patients than predictors, so the selection helps little, and the diagonal-covariance assumption ignores
the correlation between predictors, as naive Bayes does. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("pam")`, test AUC `r te_auc("pam")`.

### Tree ensembles

**Gradient boosting (`gbm`)**: Shallow trees are added one at a time, each fitted to the errors of the current logistic model, and shrunk by a learning rate. Trees find non-linear effects and interactions automatically and are unaffected by scaling,
skewness or outliers. On this cohort, however, the main signal is smooth and additive across many weak predictors, and a piecewise-constant tree needs many steps to approximate a straight-line effect. With fewer than a thousand patients the later trees
partly fit noise, so boosting is not expected to beat a penalised linear model and shows a larger gap between training and cross-validated performance. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("gbm")`, test AUC `r te_auc("gbm")`.

**Extreme gradient boosting (`xgbTree`)**: XGBoost follows the same principle but adds explicit regularisation: penalties on the leaf weights, a minimum gain to make a split (`gamma`), a minimum node weight, and row and column subsampling. These usually
make it more resistant to over-fitting than `gbm` on small data. It can exploit the age-by-performance-status interaction, but that interaction is a small part of the signal, so the gain over a linear model is limited. It is run through a custom `caret`
model because the built-in method does not work with current `xgboost` releases. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("xgbTree")`, test AUC `r te_auc("xgbTree")`.

### Neural networks

**Single-hidden-layer network (`nnet`)**: A small network combines the predictors into a few hidden units and passes them through a logistic output. Weight decay (an L2 penalty) keeps the weights small, so with few hidden units the model behaves like a
regularised logistic regression with some extra flexibility, which explains a performance close to the linear models. It needs scaled inputs (provided by the recipe) and depends on the random starting weights. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("nnet")`, test
AUC `r te_auc("nnet")`.

**Multilayer perceptron (`mlp`)**: The `RSNNS` perceptron is trained by standard back-propagation. In the tuning grid only the number of hidden units is varied, with no weight decay, so the only complexity control is the size of the hidden layer. That
means less regularisation and higher variance than `nnet`, and results that depend on random starting weights, which `set.seed()` may not fully control. Its position in the ranking is therefore less reliable. Cross-validated AUC `r cv_auc("mlp")`, test AUC
`r te_auc("mlp")`.

## 11.4 What the performance pattern shows

```{r disc-gap}
kable(gap_tbl, digits = 3,
      caption = "Cross-validated, training and test performance of each model (gaps = differences in AUC)")
```

```{r disc-family}
fam <- c(glmnet = "Linear", pls = "Linear",
         rda = "Discriminant / probabilistic", nb = "Discriminant / probabilistic",
         knn = "Distance / centroid", pam = "Distance / centroid",
         gbm = "Tree ensembles", xgbTree = "Tree ensembles",
         nnet = "Neural networks", mlp = "Neural networks")

fam_tbl <- gap_tbl %>%
  mutate(Family = unname(fam[Model])) %>%
  group_by(Family) %>%
  summarise(Models = paste(Model, collapse = ", "),
            `Mean CV AUC` = mean(`CV AUC`),
            `Mean test AUC` = mean(`Test AUC`),
            `Mean train - CV gap` = mean(`Train - CV gap`),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(`Mean CV AUC`))
best_family  <- fam_tbl$Family[1]
worst_family <- fam_tbl$Family[nrow(fam_tbl)]
kable(fam_tbl, digits = 3, caption = "Performance by model family")
```

**Differences are small:** `r length(near_best)` of the `r nrow(cv_tbl)` models are within 0.01 AUC of the best (`r paste(near_best, collapse = ", ")`). The cross-validated AUC of all models spans only `r f3(auc_range)`, while the typical fold-to-fold
standard deviation of the AUC is `r f3(fold_sd)`. Differences between the top models are therefore within noise and should not be over-interpreted.

**Family pattern**: The family with the highest mean cross-validated AUC was **`r best_family`**, and the lowest was **`r worst_family`**. This is consistent with the structure described in section 11.1: with additive effects, correlated predictors and
fewer than a thousand patients, models that shrink coefficients or share information across correlated predictors are favoured, and models that treat predictors independently (`nb`, `pam`) or rely on distances in a noisy space (`knn`) are disadvantaged.
Flexible models (trees, networks) have no structural advantage because there is little non-linearity to find.

**Over-fitting**: The gap between training and cross-validated AUC was largest for `r big_gap_model` (`r f3(big_gap)`) and smallest for `r small_gap_model` (`r f3(small_gap)`). Flexible models can reproduce the training data closely, which is why their
training AUC overstates their performance, while heavily regularised models have small gaps.

**Sensitivity versus specificity**: At the default 0.5 threshold, `r hi_spec_model` had the highest cross-validated specificity (`r f2(max(cv_tbl$Specificity))`) and `r lo_sens_model` the lowest sensitivity (`r f2(min(cv_tbl$Sensitivity))`), whereas
`r hi_sens_model` had the highest sensitivity (`r f2(max(cv_tbl$Sensitivity))`). A high specificity with a low sensitivity means that a model rarely flags a patient as high-risk. It is a property of where the model sits on its ROC curve, and it can be
changed by moving the threshold (section 10.4); the AUC is the fairer comparison.

**Test set versus cross-validation**: The Spearman correlation between the cross-validated and test AUCs across the models is `r f2(rank_cor)`. The test set has only `r nrow(te_DF)` patients, so its ranking of similar models is noisy, which is why the
final model was selected on cross-validation.

## 11.5 Practical considerations

**Interpretability**: `glmnet` provides coefficients and odds ratios; `pls` and `rda` provide weights and discriminant directions; tree ensembles and neural networks need importance measures. When several models perform equally well, the interpretable one
is preferable in a clinical setting.

**Calibration**: Logistic-type models give probabilities that can be used directly. Scores from `pls`, `knn`, `pam` and boosted trees are often mis-calibrated and may need recalibration before being read as risks.

**Cost**: `glmnet`, `pls` and `rda` train in seconds; boosted trees and networks require large tuning grids. With no accuracy benefit, the extra cost is not justified.

**Choosing among tied models**: A sensible rule is to choose the simplest model among those within one standard error of the best cross-validated AUC.

## 11.6 Limitations

**Data Used:** The data are synthetic, so this report only illustrates how to apply machine learning models. Its results are not clinical evidence, and the model must not be used to predict outcomes for real patients.

**Models Tested:** Only discrimination, calibration and threshold-based metrics were assessed. Survival models (for example Cox regression) use follow-up time and censoring, which a binary five-year outcome ignores.

**External Validation:** Validation was internal only. No external validation on an independent cohort (another hospital, country or time period) was possible, so performance in other populations is unknown.

# 12. Conclusion

Ten classification algorithms were compared with 5-fold cross-validation on a synthetic cohort of `r nrow(DF)` head and neck cancer patients. All models discriminated death within five years well above chance (cross-validated AUC from
`r f3(min(cv_tbl$ROC))` to `r f3(max(cv_tbl$ROC))`), and the leading models differed by less than the fold-to-fold variation. The selected model, **`r best_name`**, achieved a cross-validated AUC of `r f3(max(cv_tbl$ROC))` and an AUC of
`r f3(as.numeric(pROC::auc(roc_te)))` (95% CI `r f3(ci_te[1])` to `r f3(ci_te[3])`) on the held-out test set. The family with the highest mean cross-validated AUC was `r best_family`; this is consistent with a signal that is mainly additive, correlated
predictors and a small sample (section 11.1), conditions that favour regularised models over flexible ones.
